QTOPO: HOW IT WORKS

Give it a load and a bounding box.
Get back a lighter part, proven to survive.

The whole story: the problem qtopo solves, how the pipeline works, the hardware it's tested on, what's novel, and what's next. Including a real bug found and fixed this week. Every number here is sourced.

A real NASA Astrobee robot-arm mounting bracket, redesigned by this pipeline. 549 grams of titanium, down from a solid block. Now verified with a real computed safety factor, not just a stiffness number.

01. The problem

Designing a lightweight structural part is normally slow and manual.

Say you need a bracket to hold a thruster on a satellite. It must survive a real force without breaking, and weigh as little as possible. Every gram costs money to launch. The usual way: sketch a shape, simulate it, find it's too heavy or too weak, tweak by hand, repeat. Each loop takes hours. A real part can take weeks.

Topology optimization flips this. Instead of guessing a shape and checking it, you describe the constraint: load, space, material. An algorithm searches for the lightest shape that satisfies it. Not a new idea; decades-old aerospace tech. What's different here is how it's solved, and how rigorously the result gets checked. That's the rest of this page.

02. How it works

Five steps, from a real constraint to a real, printable shape.

Every step below runs on a real problem later in this page.

1

Define the real problem

A real 3D bounding box from an actual part's dimensions. A real force in Newtons, sourced from a cited document, not guessed. A real, named material with a cited stiffness and strength.

input: geometry + load + material
2

Score every tiny cell of material

The space is broken into thousands of small cells. A physics simulation (finite element analysis) scores how much each cell actually contributes to carrying the load. Some matter enormously. Most barely matter at all.

method: finite element analysis (FEA)
3

Turn "which cells to keep" into an optimization problem

"Keep the most useful X% of material, and keep neighboring cells connected" becomes a QUBO: a math format built for combinatorial optimization, and the same format quantum annealers solve.

format: QUBO (quadratic unconstrained binary optimization)
4

Solve it with whatever actually wins

Everyone assumes this step should run on a quantum computer. That assumption got tested directly (Section 04), not taken on faith. The honest answer: a classical algorithm, simulated annealing, wins every time, at every scale tried. That's what solves it today.

solver: classical simulated annealing
5

Turn the answer into a real shape

The solver's raw output is a blocky grid of yes/no cells, not something you'd manufacture. It gets smoothed into a real, watertight 3D surface, ready to print or machine.

output: watertight, manufacturable 3D mesh

04. What's actually novel

Not the algorithm alone. The discipline around trusting it.

Three things this project does that most don't.

Novel 1/3

The quantum claim was tested, not assumed.

Most "quantum-inspired optimization" companies lead with the quantum angle as the pitch. This project tested it instead: eight real solvers, two independent problem formulations, instances built to be hard, up to 800 variables.

The honest result: classical simulated annealing won every time, at every scale. Reporting that negative result plainly, instead of dropping it, is a real edge over competitors whose quantum claims have no published methodology to check.

Novel 2/3

Every bug gets found, fixed, and told.

This project keeps a dated, numbered tally of every real bug found in its own code, each with a root cause and a fix. 18 entries as of this week, not a rounded "lots of testing" claim.

Novel 3/3 · this week

The project's own physics engine had a real bug, caught by a test almost nobody runs.

Plain version: imagine a bridge simulator that passed every basic check. Internally consistent, didn't crash, looked reasonable. But nobody had run the one test that proves a simulator obeys real material law. Building a new feature required exactly that test. The simulator failed it.

The 3D engine's core stiffness matrix, transcribed from a published paper, had passed two checks: symmetry, and the right count of "rigid body" modes. Those don't catch everything. A stronger, textbook check (a "patch test": feed the simulator a case with a known correct answer) failed badly.

Old element, patch test up to 68% wrong
Rebuilt from first principles correct to machine precision

Rebuilt from scratch with the standard textbook method, no external table to mistranscribe. Verified three independent ways. The missing test is now permanent. Then put straight to work: this project's first real 3D stress verification. Not "does it look stiff enough," an actual computed stress field against a real, cited yield strength.

Real load 22.2N (NASA-calibrated)
Safety factor (upper bound) 323–340×

That large a margin is an honest finding, not a padded number. This design was optimized for stiffness, not stress, so a big margin is the expected byproduct. It points straight at the next capability (Section 06).

Note on the safety factor, added after a follow-up review: this figure is now reported as an upper bound rather than a verified value. A buckling check on a later, much thinner design found that the stress check evaluates stress at each mesh cell's centre, which for a part only one cell thick is exactly the line where bending stress is zero. Thin parts therefore under-report bending stress. The part above is thicker (2 to 6 cells) so the effect is far smaller, but it has not yet been re-measured, and saying so is more useful than leaving the number unqualified.

06. What's next

The roadmap this week's finding actually points to.

Near-term

Re-verify the other four hardware targets under the corrected physics engine

Every 3D result before this week used the flawed element. The shapes are almost certainly still sound (the corrected Astrobee re-run landed within 0.3% of the original mass). Re-running all five under the fixed engine, with real stress verification, is the concrete next step.

Next capability

Optimize for real strength, not just stiffness

This week's 323× safety factor is a direct signal: today's designs resist bending, not a target strength margin. A genuinely stress-constrained optimization (minimum mass for a chosen safety factor) should remove much more material for the same real margin.

Positioning

A verification-first alternative to unverified "quantum-inspired" platforms

Funded competitors lead with the quantum-inspired angle as marketing, with performance claims that carry no published methodology. This project's wedge isn't a faster solver. It's a habit of testing claims instead of asserting them, the same habit that caught this week's bug. That's what a technical reviewer can actually check.

Who it's for

Small-satellite teams, research labs, and early-stage hardware teams

Teams solving the exact problem this project has already solved twice: a mounting structure that must survive a real vibration environment at minimum mass. Without an in-house optimization team or a multi-week manual CAD/FEA cycle.

Real capability. Real verification. Pre-revenue, on purpose.

Nothing here is a projection or a rounded estimate. This is what's been built and tested, and, this week, a real mistake caught and fixed. Stated plainly, not smoothed over. That's the whole pitch.
